doc.title: Jackie Williams interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, October 18, 1995

chapter: Influences and the future of jazz
title: Why young players need more outlets; a European big band festival
summary: He wants more outlets for young talent, recalls how dances and varied jobs trained earlier players, and describes a packed European big band festival.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: There’s a lot of young and really good talent. I mean these kinds are just, they’re on the money you know. They’ve really got some talent. And it would be just so wonderful if they had a place to really let it out you know, in the right way you know. Because it’s not always in the book. It’s not always in the studio. You see what I mean? It’s not always, see what made the Joe Williams and Buddy Riches, the Jo Jones and Gene Krupa, they had a whole spectrum of outlets. They had the dances, you know, they had the carnivals and circuses and all that stuff. They got experiences from a lot of different sources you know? Movies. And you’ve got, that dance thing was important to give you a sense of moods and emotions you know? You could play something and it’s not always going to be, rippity, rippity, you know, fast and exciting, because people are not always in that mood. So that’s the good thing about the dance, dancing, you know the dance halls and stuff like that. That was very good. And it brought people together a lot you know. You get a chance to socialize and it was great. But it’s really nice today also. But I’ll tell you one thing, over in Europe they believe, and they have a — I was over there last, the year before last with the Alden-Barrett quintet which I recommend, when we get a chance. And we went to, they had a wonderful — we played a festival over there and one of the days they had a great festival of the big band era. They had Lionel Hampton was there and then they had a band, I forget who the leader was but it was based on Glenn Miller — it was the Glenn Miller band actually. But they played all the other big bands. The Glenn Miller band played the music of Duke Ellington, they played the music of Count Basie, they played the music of Tommy Dorsey, and they played wonderful. They just played, you know all the tunes, a lot of the music that you were familiar with with those particular bands. And that band played so good. And naturally Lionel Hampton’s band just wiped everybody out. They just tore the whole place up. The just wiped everybody out. But that Glenn Miller band was very good. And it was good to see. And that place was packed — jammed. And there was young, there was old, and they was dancing. It looked like something from out of the 40s or the 50s. It was unbelievable. Everybody did all complimenting about that. And it was just beautiful. Now that’s the kind of things they need to bring out more I think here. And that would really balance out that whole thing. Because they didn’t lose that you see? Over there they cherish all of that stuff you know.
That’s interesting. A lot of people have said that. I don’t know, sometimes when an art form comes from somewhere else, people treat it with more respect.

They treat that with a great deal of respect. And they look forward to that particular time every year. They come out and people tell me they get stronger and stronger. And I could see that for myself. Those people were out. And all age groups. It wasn’t just the people that are over 50 and 60. These are the youngsters you know?
